adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — On rebalance, strategy.close() shuts down the factory-owned shared queue_pool, so the next strategy from create_with_partitions reuses dead queues; put() raises queue.ShutDown, submit's except marks the offset complete, and the commit loop commits every later message unprocessed (silent data loss after the first rebalance).

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ResultsStrategyFactory creates a single shared `queue_pool` in `__init__` for mode `thread-queue-parallel` and reuses it in every `create_with_partitions` call (`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` passes `self.queue_pool`). But `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` always calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down workers and calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` on each underlying `queue.Queue`. The factory does not recreate `queue_pool` after a strategy is closed; it only sets it to `None` in `factory.shutdown()`. Therefore, if the processing framework closes a strategy and later asks the same factory to create a new strategy (e.g., after a rebalance), the new strategy will reuse a shut-down pool; subsequent `queue_pool.submit()` will call `work_queue.put(work_item)` on a shutdown queue (raising `queue.ShutDown`), which is caught by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`'s broad `except Exception`, and it then `add_offset` + `complete_offset`, making the commit loop consider the message processed and eligible for commit without running `result_processor` (silent data loss).

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:317 — submit() swallows every exception (including queue.ShutDown and grouping_fn errors) and then marks the offset complete, so dropped messages get committed as if they were processed.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the entire decode/group/queueing path is wrapped in `except Exception:`. On any exception (e.g., `grouping_fn` raising, or `queue_pool.submit` / `work_queue.put` raising such as `queue.ShutDown` after shutdown), the handler logs and then calls `offset_tracker.add_offset(...)` and `complete_offset(...)`. That makes the offset immediately committable even though the message was not processed/enqueued, so the commit loop can commit past a dropped message (data loss). This behavior is directly visible in the added `submit` implementation in `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — Queues are unbounded and submit never blocks or raises MessageRejected, so there is no backpressure (despite what the docstring says): when processing is slower than consumption, memory grows without limit until OOM.

adjudication.rationale: The new FixedQueuePool creates each queue with `queue.Queue()` (default `maxsize=0`, i.e., unbounded) and `submit()` always does `work_queue.put(work_item)` without any rejection path (no maxsize, no `MessageRejected`). This means ingestion can outpace processing indefinitely and memory can grow without bound, contradicting the strategy docstring claim of “Natural backpressure when queues fill up.” This resource-exhaustion risk is a real defect introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:287 — The arroyo Commit callback (stage_offsets/commit_offsets, commit-policy state, DLQ buffer) is called from a background thread while the StreamProcessor main thread is polling or rebalancing; arroyo strategies are expected to commit from the consumer thread, so this can race internal state or stage offsets for partitions being revoked.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly shows the new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` starts a background `commit_thread` in `__init__` and calls `self.commit_function(committable)` from `_commit_loop` (queue_consumer.py). In `ResultsStrategyFactory.create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`, `commit_function` directly calls the Arroyo `commit(...)` callback. So the commit callback is indeed invoked from a non-consumer/background thread. However, the claim that Arroyo *requires* commits only from the StreamProcessor consumer thread (and that this definitively races internal commit-policy/DLQ state) is not something that can be conclusively verified from the diff alone; what is verifiable is the cross-thread commit behavior and the associated concurrency/architecture risk introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:89 — The committable scan requires every offset in the range to have been seen, so any gap in Kafka offsets (compaction, transaction control records) stops commits on that partition for good while all_offsets grows without limit.

adjudication.rationale: In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets`, the committable scan iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` and *breaks* if any `offset` is not present in `all_offsets` (the `if offset in all_offsets and offset not in outstanding` check). That means commits can only advance across a fully contiguous sequence of offsets that were observed via `add_offset`. If the consumer ever experiences an unseen offset gap on a partition (i.e., some offsets exist in Kafka but never reach `submit`/`add_offset`), `highest_committable` will stop at the last contiguous seen offset and never progress. In that stuck state, `mark_committed` is never called for higher offsets, so `all_offsets[partition]` is never pruned and will grow without bound as more messages are processed on that partition.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:44 — The shared OffsetTracker is never cleared for revoked partitions: an offset abandoned in a queue at shutdown stays outstanding, and if the partition comes back later at a higher offset, min(all_offsets) points at the stale offset and commits for that partition stall forever.

adjudication.rationale: In `queue_consumer.py`, `OffsetTracker` retains `all_offsets`/`outstanding` per `Partition` and has no API or call site to clear state for a partition when processing is stopped (e.g., rebalance/revocation or shutdown with queued work). `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, so workers may exit without draining queued `WorkItem`s, leaving their offsets in `outstanding` forever. If that same `OffsetTracker`/`FixedQueuePool` is reused later for the same partition (the factory stores `self.queue_pool` and reuses it in `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`), `get_committable_offsets()` will start from `min(all_offsets)` and will break on the stale outstanding offset, preventing commits for that partition indefinitely.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:129 — Setting worker.shutdown=True before q.shutdown(immediate=False) makes workers exit after their current item and abandon the queued backlog, and close() does no final commit after workers finish, so revocation or shutdown redelivers work processed after the last commit tick.

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, the code sets `worker.shutdown = True` before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, the main loop is `while not self.shutdown:`; once `shutdown` is set, a worker will exit after finishing its current item and will not continue draining remaining queued items, leaving backlog unprocessed. Additionally, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops the commit loop first (`shutdown_event.set()` + `commit_thread.join(...)`) and only then shuts down the queue pool, with no final commit after workers finish; this can leave already-processed offsets uncommitted at shutdown, causing redelivery after revocation/restart.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:89 — The contiguity scan breaks on the first missing offset, so any gap in Kafka offsets (transaction markers or compaction) permanently stops commits for that partition

adjudication.rationale: In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets`, the scan does break on the first offset in `range(start, max_offset + 1)` that is either outstanding or not present in `all_offsets`. However, this does **not** permanently stop commits when Kafka offsets have gaps: after committing up to the last processed offset before the gap, `mark_committed` updates `last_committed` and removes `<= committed` from `all_offsets`, and `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` then jumps forward to `min_offset` (which can be greater than the missing offset). That allows later offsets to become committable even if the missing offset never appears. So the claimed “permanently stops commits for that partition” is not supported by the diff’s logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:335 — close()/join() skip the final commit of completed offsets and don't drain the queued work, so up to a second of processed results plus all queued items get reprocessed after a rebalance or restart

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`, it sets `shutdown_event` and then joins the commit thread (`commit_thread.join(timeout=5.0)`). The commit loop is `while not self.shutdown_event.is_set(): ... wait(1.0) ... commit`, so setting the event can cause the loop to exit at the next iteration boundary without performing a final `get_committable_offsets()`/`commit_function()` pass, leaving up to the last ~1s of completed offsets uncommitted. Additionally, `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, and `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loops `while not self.shutdown:`; this ordering causes workers to stop processing immediately rather than draining queued items, so queued work will remain unprocessed and offsets won’t be completed/committed, leading to reprocessing after restart/rebalance.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:133 — FixedQueuePool is created once in the factory but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (queue_consumer.py:338) shuts it down, so ownership is unclear and a strategy recreated after rebalance gets a pool with dead workers and closed queues

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates and stores a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` when `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"` (result_consumer.py). `create_with_partitions` then passes that same factory-owned pool into each new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` instance. The factory does not recreate the pool on subsequent `create_with_partitions` calls unless the whole factory is re-instantiated, and `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` asserts only that `self.queue_pool is not None`, not that it is live. Therefore a strategy lifecycle event (e.g., close on rebalance) can leave the factory holding a non-None but dead pool, and subsequent strategies will reuse it, causing broken processing/commits.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:278 — The strategy reaches through queue_pool.offset_tracker in several places (278, 289, 302-303, 320-325) instead of calling a pool API, which couples it to the pool's internals

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:344 — join() ignores its timeout and just calls close(), and terminate() skips joining the commit thread, which misrepresents arroyo's ProcessingStrategy contract

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`, `join(self, timeout: float | None = None)` ignores the provided `timeout` and unconditionally calls `self.close()`, which itself blocks on `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` and `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`. adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:249 — The "+1 next offset" commit conversion lives in the factory while OffsetTracker returns last-processed offsets, which splits offset semantics across the module boundary

adjudication.rationale: In `queue_consumer.py`, `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()` returns the highest *processed* offset (e.g., `highest_committable = offset`), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` forwards that directly to `commit_function(committable)` and then calls `mark_committed(partition, offset)` with the same value. adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:47 — OffsetTracker never evicts per-partition state (all_offsets, outstanding, last_committed, locks) on partition revocation, and the class docstring does not mention this lifecycle

Even when offsets are fully committed, `mark_committed` only filters `all_offsets` and does not remove the partition entry, and `get_committable_offsets` does not evict empty partitions either. There is also no API to clear state on a lifecycle event like partition revocation/rebalance. The diff does not show whether partition revocation occurs or whether strategies are recreated on rebalance, so this is best treated as a lifecycle/maintenance concern rather than a verifiable functional bug from the diff alone; the docstring also doesn’t mention the lack of eviction.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — Work queues are unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit` never blocks or raises MessageRejected, so there is no backpressure (contrary to the docstring at line 253) and a slow worker lets the consumer pull Kafka unboundedly into memory

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, so it is effectively unbounded. In `FixedQueuePool.submit`, it unconditionally does `work_queue.put(work_item)` (which will not block in practice for an unbounded queue) and never raises `MessageRejected` or otherwise signals upstream to slow down. This contradicts the `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring claim of “Natural backpressure when queues fill up” and allows the consumer to buffer arbitrarily many Kafka messages in memory if workers fall behind (risking unbounded memory growth).

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:31 — WorkItem retains the full arroyo Message (raw KafkaPayload bytes) alongside the decoded result though it is never used, roughly doubling per-item memory in the unbounded queues

adjudication.rationale: In `queue_consumer.py`, `WorkItem` includes `message: Message[...]`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` populates it (`message=message`). However, downstream processing (`OrderedQueueWorker.run`) only uses `work_item.result` and offset tracking uses `partition`/`offset`; `work_item.message` is never referenced anywhere in this diff. Also, `FixedQueuePool` uses `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, so it is unbounded. Keeping the full `Message` (with raw payload) per enqueued item is a concrete, diff-grounded memory/architecture concern, though not a correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:83 — get_committable_offsets does O(n) min()/max() over the full all_offsets set plus a per-offset range walk every second while holding the partition lock, contending with add_offset/complete_offset on the hot path and scaling with backlog size

adjudication.rationale: In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets`, the diff shows it acquires the per-partition lock and then computes `min(all_offsets)` and `max(all_offsets)` on a `set[int]`, and then walks `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` checking membership in `all_offsets`/`outstanding` (both sets). This work is done while holding the same lock used by the hot-path methods `add_offset`/`complete_offset` (also under `_get_partition_lock`). The commit loop in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` calls `get_committable_offsets()` every second, so the lock hold time and overall work scale with backlog size and can contend with producers/completers. This is a real, diff-grounded scalability/performance issue, not a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:105 — mark_committed rebuilds the entire all_offsets set via comprehension under the partition lock on every commit (O(n) copy and allocation) instead of incremental removal

adjudication.rationale: In `OffsetTracker.mark_committed`, the diff shows `self.all_offsets[partition] = {o for o in self.all_offsets[partition] if o > offset}`, which rebuilds the entire set (O(n) time and allocation) while holding the per-partition lock. This is a real, diff-grounded performance/scalability concern, but not a correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:89 — Commit scan breaks on any offset missing from all_offsets, so non-contiguous Kafka offsets (transaction markers or compaction gaps) permanently stall commits and let all_offsets grow without bound

adjudication.rationale: In OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets(), the scan does `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` and immediately `break`s if an offset is either not in `all_offsets` or still outstanding. Since `all_offsets` only contains offsets that were explicitly `add_offset`’d (i.e., messages the consumer actually saw), any real gap in the consumed stream (an offset that will never be observed/added) will cause the scan to stop at the first missing offset and prevent committing later processed offsets. In that situation, `last_committed` never advances and `all_offsets[partition]` cannot be pruned via mark_committed(), so it can grow without bound.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:150 — Each worker emits a metrics.gauge plus a locked qsize() call in `finally` for every message processed, adding per-message metrics overhead across all worker threads

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run` the `finally` block runs for every processed item and calls `metrics.gauge(...)` with `self.work_queue.qsize()`. This adds per-message metrics emission and a `qsize()` call (which can take an internal lock and is documented as potentially expensive/approximate) across all worker threads. This is a concrete performance/overhead concern visible in the diff, but it does not represent a correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:328 — poll(), which arroyo calls very frequently, runs get_stats() each time, taking every queue's mutex for qsize(), building a list and emitting a gauge metric, with no rate limiting

adjudication.rationale: In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll() unconditionally calls self.queue_pool.get_stats() and then emits a gauge every time poll() is invoked. get_stats() iterates all queues and calls q.qsize() for each (building a full list of depths) and sums them. This is a concrete per-poll O(num_queues) operation with repeated qsize() calls (which in CPython’s queue.Queue are synchronized). The diff does not show any rate limiting or sampling, so the performance concern is diff-grounded, though the claim about arroyo calling poll “very frequently” is external to the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:202 — Static `hash(group_key) % num_queues` assignment with a single worker per queue means one hot or slow subscription blocks every other group on that queue (head-of-line blocking) and holds back commits for the whole partition

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` and each queue has exactly one `OrderedQueueWorker` thread (single consumer per queue). This design can cause head-of-line blocking within a queue: a “hot” or slow group mapped to a queue will delay processing of other groups mapped to that same queue because they share the same FIFO worker. Additionally, because `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()` only advances commits once earlier offsets in a partition are completed, any slow/outstanding earlier offset in that partition will prevent committing later offsets (even if later messages were processed on other queues). This is a real performance/throughput/fairness concern created by the change, but it is not a correctness defect per se since Kafka commits are inherently ordered per partition and the strategy appears intentionally designed to preserve per-group ordering.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:47 — Per-partition locks and offset dicts (partition_locks, all_offsets, outstanding, last_committed) are never cleaned up on partition revocation, so they grow with rebalances

adjudication.rationale: OffsetTracker stores per-partition state in `all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed`, and `partition_locks` and the diff does not add any mechanism to remove entries when a partition is no longer assigned (no “revoke/cleanup” API; `mark_committed` only prunes old offsets within `all_offsets` and does not delete partition keys or clear other dicts). That said, the finding’s claim that this will “grow with rebalances” is not strictly demonstrated by the diff: `Partition` keys are value-equal (topic/index), so repeated rebalances over the same finite partition set won’t create unbounded new keys, though stale per-partition entries can remain if partitions change over the process lifetime.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:243 — Shutdown joins each worker one after another with a 5s timeout, so it can take up to num_queues*5s (100s by default) and may exceed rebalance or shutdown deadlines

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (queue_consumer.py), workers are joined in a loop with `worker.join(timeout=5.0)`. Because this is done sequentially for every worker, the total shutdown wait can be up to `num_queues * 5s` in the worst case (default `num_queues=20` => up to ~100s). The diff does not show explicit rebalance/shutdown deadlines being violated, so this is a real, diff-grounded operational concern rather than a guaranteed correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — Strategy close() on rebalance shuts down the factory-shared FixedQueuePool, so the next strategy from create_with_partitions (result_consumer.py:247 assert still passes) gets queue.ShutDown on every put, which submit() catches and marks complete, silently dropping and committing all later messages.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `ResultsStrategyFactory` creates a single `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__` for `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"` and reuses it across strategies (`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` passes `queue_pool=self.queue_pool` and only asserts it is not `None`). adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:287 — The Arroyo commit callable is called from a background thread while the main thread polls or rebalances (StreamProcessor/KafkaConsumer state is not thread-safe), and stale revoked partitions in the shared OffsetTracker make stage_offsets raise "unassigned partitions" on every loop, so commits stall for all partitions (only logged).

adjudication.rationale: The new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` starts a dedicated background `commit_thread` in `__init__` that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)` (`_commit_loop`). In `ResultsStrategyFactory.create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`, `commit_function` ultimately calls the Arroyo `commit` callable. This means commits happen off the main processor thread, while `StreamProcessor`/consumer polling and potential rebalances happen elsewhere; the diff provides no synchronization or rebalance hooks to make this safe. Additionally, `OffsetTracker` retains per-`Partition` state indefinitely unless offsets are committed (`mark_committed`) and has no mechanism to clear state when partitions are revoked/reassigned, so after a rebalance it can still attempt to commit offsets for partitions that may no longer be assigned. adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — Work queues are unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize) and submit never blocks or raises MessageRejected, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring; a slow processor lets memory and OffsetTracker state grow until OOM.

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, making it effectively unbounded. In `FixedQueuePool.submit`, it always calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` after `offset_tracker.add_offset(...)`; with an unbounded queue, `put` will not apply backpressure. This contradicts `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring claim of “Natural backpressure when queues fill up” and allows queue memory (and `OffsetTracker`’s `all_offsets/outstanding` sets) to grow without bound if processing is slow, risking OOM.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:44 — OffsetTracker is never reset or pruned for revoked partitions across rebalances, so outstanding offsets and last_committed for partitions the consumer no longer owns persist and get committed or processed after reassignment.

adjudication.rationale: In `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, `queue_pool` (and its `OffsetTracker`) is created once and stored on the factory (`self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`). `create_with_partitions` then returns a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` that reuses this same `queue_pool` across calls. `OffsetTracker` stores `all_offsets/outstanding/last_committed` keyed by `Partition` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` blindly commits whatever `get_committable_offsets()` returns for *all* partitions present in the tracker; there is no API or logic in the diff to clear state for partitions that are no longer assigned after a rebalance/revocation. Because `factory.shutdown()` is the only place that shuts down/clears the pool, a rebalance that recreates the strategy can leave old partition offsets/items in the shared pool/tracker and the new strategy can continue processing/committing them even if the consumer no longer owns those partitions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:344 — join(timeout) ignores its timeout and neither drains the queues nor does a final commit, so on graceful shutdown or rebalance all queued and completed-but-uncommitted work is abandoned and reprocessed (up to 1s plus the whole backlog).

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout=None)`, the `timeout` parameter is ignored because it unconditionally calls `self.close()` (no use of `timeout`). More importantly, `close()` sets `shutdown_event` and joins the commit thread, then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`. `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for each worker; since `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loops `while not self.shutdown:`, workers may exit immediately without draining any queued items. There is also no explicit drain/wait-for-empty or “final commit” on shutdown; the commit loop runs periodically and can stop once `shutdown_event` is set, leaving completed-but-uncommitted offsets uncommitted. This can cause queued work and already-processed work to be reprocessed after shutdown/rebalance (up to the commit interval plus backlog).

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:243 — Workers are joined one after another with 5s each (up to 100s for 20 queues) plus a 5s commit-thread join, all inside Arroyo's revoke callback, which can exceed max.poll.interval or the pod termination grace period when a processor is blocked on I/O.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds shutdown logic that can block for a long time: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` sets the shutdown event then does `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` and calls `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, workers are joined sequentially with `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` in a loop, so worst-case blocking time is roughly `num_queues * 5s` (default `num_queues=20` in `FixedQueuePool.__init__`) plus the commit thread join. This is a real operational risk (slow partition revoke/shutdown, potentially exceeding external timeouts), even if it’s not a correctness defect per se. The claim that it’s specifically inside Arroyo’s revoke callback / exceeding `max.poll.interval` isn’t directly shown in the diff, but the blocking behavior itself is verifiable here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:340 — terminate() does not join the commit thread and close() tolerates a join timeout, so an orphaned commit loop can call a stale commit callable after the strategy is closed or the consumer is shutting down.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`, a daemon `commit_thread` is started in `__init__` and runs `_commit_loop` calling `self.commit_function(...)`. `close()` sets `shutdown_event` but only `join(timeout=5.0)`, so if the commit loop is blocked inside `commit_function` (or otherwise doesn’t exit promptly), `close()` can return with the thread still alive. `terminate()` sets `shutdown_event` and shuts down the pool but never joins the `commit_thread` at all, making it even more likely the commit loop can outlive strategy shutdown and still invoke the commit callable during/after shutdown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:149 — Worker threads are daemon threads with no supervision: an exception escaping run() (for example from the finally block or a BaseException) kills the worker permanently, its queue grows forever and that partition's commits stall with no alert.

adjudication.rationale: The new `OrderedQueueWorker` threads are started as daemon threads (`super().__init__(daemon=True)`) and there is no monitoring/restart mechanism in `FixedQueuePool` if a worker thread dies. If a worker were to terminate unexpectedly, its queue would stop draining and offsets for those work items would never be marked complete, which would block `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()` progress and stall commits. However, the finding overstates the likelihood: `run()` does catch `Exception` around `result_processor(...)`, so ordinary exceptions from processing won't “escape run()” and permanently kill the worker; only `BaseException` or an unexpected exception outside that try/except (e.g., in the `finally` block) would.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:132 — The code relies on queue.ShutDown and Queue.shutdown (Python 3.13+); on an older runtime, shutdown errors are only logged and workers stay blocked in get() forever, so shutdown always hits the join timeouts.

adjudication.rationale: The new implementation in `queue_consumer.py` explicitly references `queue.ShutDown` in `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` (two `except queue.ShutDown:` blocks) and calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`. These APIs are not present on older Python versions (pre-3.13), so on such runtimes `q.shutdown(...)` will raise and be swallowed (only logged), and workers will remain blocked on `work_queue.get()` (no timeout) even after `worker.shutdown = True`, causing shutdown to rely on `join(timeout=5.0)` timeouts. This is a concrete behavioral defect/compatibility break introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:253 — No test covers close() followed by create_with_partitions (a rebalance): close() shuts down the factory's shared queue_pool, so the next strategy's put() raises ShutDown, submit swallows it and marks the offset complete, and messages get committed without being processed

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `ResultsStrategyFactory` creates a single shared `queue_pool` in `__init__` when `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"` and then reuses it for every `create_with_partitions` call. However `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` always calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down the underlying Python `queue.Queue` instances via `q.shutdown(...)`. If the same factory later calls `create_with_partitions` again (e.g., after a rebalance) it will return a new strategy that uses the already-shutdown `queue_pool`; subsequent `FixedQueuePool.submit()` will call `work_queue.put(...)` which can raise `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches `Exception` and then marks the offset complete (`add_offset` + `complete_offset`), allowing the commit loop to commit offsets for messages that were never processed. The tests added do not cover this close→recreate scenario.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:312 — test_preserves_order_within_group only asserts len==5 and never checks processing order, so it passes even if ordering is broken

adjudication.rationale: In tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py, TestSimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.test_preserves_order_within_group submits 5 messages for the same group ("sub1") but only asserts processing completed and `len(self.processed_results) == 5`. It never checks that the processed results arrived in the same order as offsets, despite the test name and the strategy’s stated ordering guarantees. This is a specific, diff-grounded test gap rather than a functional defect in the implementation itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:200 — Asserting total_items > 0 right after submit races with the worker threads, which may already have drained all queues (qsize drops on get), so the test is flaky

adjudication.rationale: In `TestFixedQueuePool.test_stats_reporting`, the test submits 10 items and then immediately calls `stats = self.pool.get_stats()` and asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. However, `FixedQueuePool` starts daemon `OrderedQueueWorker` threads in its constructor, and those workers call `work_queue.get()` which reduces `qsize()` immediately. It is therefore possible for all items to be drained (and even processed) before the stats check, making `total_items` equal to 0 and causing a flaky failure. This race is directly implied by the diff: queues are unbounded and workers run continuously as soon as the pool is constructed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:2005 — test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown only asserts queue_pool is None; it never checks that the queued items were drained or processed, and it runs the real processor on worker threads outside the test DB transaction and outside the feature-flag context

adjudication.rationale: In `test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown`, the test enqueues 5 messages via `self.send_result(...)` and then only asserts `factory.queue_pool is None` after `factory.shutdown()`. It does not assert that any queued items were processed or drained before shutdown. This is especially relevant because `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` calls `queue_pool.shutdown()` (which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, shuts down the queues, and joins threads) without any explicit “drain before stopping” assertion in the test. Also, unlike the other new tests, this one does not patch/mocks `type(factory.result_processor).__call__`, so the real `result_processor` will execute on background worker threads (`OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `self.result_processor(...)`), which can escape the test’s normal synchronous control and can be risky in Django tests. This is a test coverage/robustness concern rather than a proven product defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1699 — Every thread-queue-parallel test mocks result_processor.__call__ and asserts on mock calls, so real result handling (DB access and feature flags from worker threads) is never exercised in the new mode; ProcessResultTest has no thread-queue-parallel subclass

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:351 — No coverage for the decoder raising (submit's except branch), commit_function raising in _commit_loop, or offsets from multiple partitions interleaving through the strategy

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds nontrivial error-handling paths in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`: `submit()` wraps `decoder(...)` and the rest of submission in a broad `except Exception:` that marks offsets complete (queue_consumer.py), and `_commit_loop()` also wraps commit handling in `except Exception:`. The new tests in `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py` cover normal processing, filtered payloads (`result is None` path), offset gaps, and multiple partitions only at the `OffsetTracker` level, but do not exercise: (1) `decoder` raising to hit `submit`'s exception branch, (2) `commit_function` raising to hit `_commit_loop`'s exception handling, or (3) offset tracking/committing behavior when messages from multiple partitions interleave through the *strategy* (as opposed to tracker-only tests). This is a concrete, diff-grounded missing-test issue rather than a verified runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:348 — commit_event fires on any commit tick, so a tick that lands between the offset-100 completion and the offset-101 processing (and likewise mid-batch at line 297) leaves a partial committed offset and makes the equality assertion flaky

In `test_offset_committing` the test waits for `process_complete_event` (all items processed) but then `commit_event.wait()` can return immediately due to an earlier partial commit, and the assertion `self.committed_offsets[partition] == 104` can observe an earlier value (e.g., 100/101/...). adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1864 — The wait loop breaks on the first commit of any size, then asserts ==105 immediately, so an early partial commit makes the test flaky

adjudication.rationale: In `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit`, the wait loop breaks as soon as `stats["total_items"] == 0` and *any* commit has occurred (`len(committed_offsets) > 0`). Since commits happen asynchronously in a background commit loop and may advance in multiple steps (partial commits before the final offset), this can exit before the final commit is observed, then immediately asserts `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 105`, making the test potentially flaky.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:106 — test_different_groups_distributed depends on randomized str hash() (PYTHONHASHSEED), so there is a small nondeterministic chance that 20 keys miss one of the 3 buckets

adjudication.rationale: In tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py::test_different_groups_distributed, the assertion `assert len(queue_indices) == 3` depends on `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group`, which uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python’s `hash()` for strings is salted per-process (PYTHONHASHSEED), and even within one run there is no guarantee that 20 chosen keys will hit all 3 buckets. This makes the test potentially flaky/nondeterministic, even if low probability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:2140 — verify_consumer.close() and the processor/factory shutdown are not in finally blocks, so a failed assertion leaks Kafka consumers and worker threads; the fixed 5s _run_once loop also slows the suite
